source.title: How Does Disagreement Benefit Co-teaching?
source.authors: Xing-Rui Yu; Bo Han; Jiangchao Yao; Gang Niu; I. Tsang; Masashi Sugiyama

record.tranche_reason: The paper relies on deep-network memorization to motivate Co-teaching+, but its reported experiments evaluate noisy-label learning methods rather than testing whether standard networks fit completely random labels or the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper describes Standard-model test-accuracy curves on fixed noisy-label datasets and discusses memorization as training progresses. These do not measure the behaviors named in V1–V6. References to Zhang et al. (2017) and Arpit et al. (2017) are cited prior work, not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The Standard baselines provide qualitative evidence on V6: Section 3.2 reports initially high test accuracy followed by deterioration during training, explicitly interpreting this as learning clean labels before overfitting noisy labels. This is indirect evidence from generalization curves rather than separate measurements of clean-label and noisy-label fitting. The study also uses memorization to motivate Co-teaching+.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that Co-teaching+ improves robustness under noisy supervision and identify small-loss selection, cross-updating, and maintaining divergence as key factors. Their own Standard-baseline results also qualitatively illustrate early learning of clean signal followed by overfitting noise.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes Co-teaching+, a noisy-label training method using disagreement filtering and cross-updates; it does not reproduce the original random-label experiments.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 97, 2019
record.problems: Standard-model outcomes are shown only in figures in the supplied text, without numerical values or uncertainty estimates; its experiments do not test the random-label fitting claims.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and comparison with true-label training under unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training time to fit random versus true labels and convergence slowdown as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training-set fitting across corruption rates from none to all and steady test-error degradation toward chance. The tested noise levels and test accuracies alone do not establish this joint claim.
Effects of adding or removing weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Direct trajectories of fitting clean versus corrupted training examples, and comparison of learning dynamics on fully real versus fully random labels.

record.verdict_notes: No numerical curve values can be recovered from the supplied text, but Section 3.2 explicitly describes the relevant temporal behavior. These descriptions justify qualitative V6 verdicts; they do not establish zero training error or directly isolate memorization of corrupted examples. Final test-accuracy tables and network-divergence measurements add no direct evidence for the other versions.

versions.untested_parts: Whether standard networks fit completely random training labels with test error at chance without changing architecture or hyperparameters.
Relative training time for random versus true labels and convergence slowdown as corruption rises.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Whether training error remains perfect as label corruption rises from none to all, and whether test error rises steadily toward chance.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation affect fitting random labels or true-label generalization.
Whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels, or whether real and random labels are learned differently.
